summary: On 2 July 2019 one new firewall rule with a badly written regular expression pushed CPU to the limit on every Cloudflare edge server at once. Customers saw 502 error pages for about 27 minutes.

overview.background: Cloudflare runs a web application firewall (WAF) at every edge location. Managed Rules are updated many times a week so new attacks can be blocked fast, so these updates do not go through the staged rollout used for other software.
systems: WAF Managed Rules on every edge server
HTTP and HTTPS serving on the edge (CPU shared with the WAF)
overview.impact: Customers and their visitors saw a 502 error page when visiting any Cloudflare-proxied domain. Cloudflare reports that the outage lasted 27 minutes.
overview.severity: Global. Every Cloudflare edge location was affected. Cloudflare does not publish a numeric severity rating.
overview.gaps: The post does not give the exact time the outage ended, the exact time of the first page, or when each status update was made. The WAF rule text is only shown in simplified form.

archNote: Components and the rule-deployment path are described in Cloudflare's post. The layout and arrow labels are ours.

diagrams.title: A WAF rule change reaches every edge at once
diagrams.caption: Managed Rules bypass the staged rollout used for normal software, so one bad rule reached all edge servers within minutes and used up the CPU that serves traffic.

diagrams.title: Staged rule rollout with CPU protection (conceptual)
diagrams.caption: Cloudflare said it would add performance profiling to its tests, use a regex engine without this behaviour, stage WAF rules like other software, and restore the CPU protection. This picture is our illustration of those steps.

nodes.label: Engineer merges a WAF rule change
CPU protection and linear-time regex engine

afterChanges: A slow rule is caught by a performance test before it ships.
If one gets through, it reaches a small canary first, not the whole world.
A regex engine with guaranteed linear time cannot backtrack catastrophically.
Per-request CPU protection limits the harm of any single rule.
afterNote: The change is about blast radius and early detection, not only about writing better expressions.
timelineNote: All times are UTC on 2 July 2019, as written in the Cloudflare post. The first-page time is derived from the post saying the page went out three minutes after the deployment.

timeline.e: An engineer merges a pull request containing the WAF change after it is approved.
The build system builds the rules and runs the tests, which pass.
An engineer on the firewall team deploys the change. The rule reaches all edge servers.
The first PagerDuty page goes out, three minutes after the deployment.
The WAF is identified as the component causing the problem.
The team discusses a global terminate of the WAF, a step normally avoided.
A team member executes the global WAF termination.
Traffic levels and CPU are back to expected levels worldwide.
Cloudflare is satisfied that it understands the cause and has a fix in place.

rootCause.trigger: A new WAF Managed Rule containing a poorly written regular expression was deployed globally.
rootCause.underlying: The expression backtracked enormously on some input and used up the CPU that serves HTTP and HTTPS traffic. The rule was run by a regex engine that can take time that grows very fast with input length.
contributing: The standard procedure let a non-emergency rule change go to production worldwide without a staged rollout
Tests did not check the rule's CPU cost
An earlier change had removed a protection that limited CPU use by regular expressions
Using the global WAF kill switch was a step the team had to stop and discuss before taking
The status page was not updated quickly enough
propagation: The rule reaches every edge server within minutes.
Each request that touches the rule burns CPU.
Serving capacity falls, and the front-line web servers that still have cores available return 502 errors.
Customers and their visitors see errors on any Cloudflare domain.

evidence.label: What exhausted the CPU
evidence.body: a regular expression that backtracked enormously and exhausted CPU used for HTTP/HTTPS serving
evidence.note: From Cloudflare's post. The post's appendix reduces the critical part of the pattern to .*.*=.*

evidence.label: What visitors saw
evidence.body: seeing a 502 error page when visiting any Cloudflare domain

evidence.label: Why the pattern is dangerous
evidence.body:
python3 - <<'EOF'
import re, time
for n in (500, 1000, 2000):
    s = 'x' * n          # no '=' anywhere, so the match must fail
    t = time.time(); re.search(r'.*.*=.*', s)
    print(n, round(time.time() - t, 3), 'seconds')
EOF
evidence.note: A teaching experiment, not Cloudflare output. In our run with Python's re module, each doubling of input made the match roughly eight times slower. Other regex engines behave differently, which is the point of the fix.

evidence.label: What a CPU alert might show
evidence.body:
ALERT edge-cpu-high  region=all  value=99%  for=2m
ALERT http-5xx-rate  region=all  value=82%  for=2m
evidence.note: Illustrative alert text. The post does not publish alert definitions.

diagnose.step: Compare the timing of the CPU rise with the last deployment.
diagnose.why: A rise that starts minutes after a deploy points at the deploy, not at traffic.

diagnose.step: Find which component uses the CPU.
diagnose.why: Profile the busy processes to find the hot function.

diagnose.step: Isolate the component with a feature switch rather than guessing.
diagnose.why: Turning off one suspect and watching CPU fall is stronger evidence than any theory.

correct.step: Disable the suspect component globally using the kill switch.
correct.why: Restoring service first is the priority. You can lose some protection for a short time and repair it after.

correct.step: Confirm CPU and error rates fall.
correct.why: Recovery should be visible within minutes if the diagnosis is right.

correct.step: Fix or remove the bad rule, then re-enable in stages.
correct.why: Re-enabling everywhere at once would repeat the outage if the fix is wrong.

verify.step: Replay recent traffic against the fixed rule in a test environment and record CPU.
verify.why: A rule must prove it is cheap on real inputs, not only correct on examples.

verify.step: Watch 5xx rate and CPU across all regions after each stage.
verify.why: Stages catch what a test cannot.

prevent.step: Add a performance profile to the rule tests with a hard CPU budget.
prevent.why: A rule that works but is slow still causes an outage.

prevent.step: Use a regular expression engine with linear running time, or put a per-request time limit around matching.
prevent.why: Catastrophic backtracking becomes impossible or bounded.

prevent.step: Roll rule changes out in stages like any other software, with a faster lane for real emergencies.
prevent.why: Speed matters for attacks, but a bad rule is also an emergency.

fix.safety: A global kill switch removes protection for every customer. Agree in advance who may use it and how it is announced, then practise it so nobody hesitates when it matters.

troubleshoot.scenario: Five minutes after a deploy, CPU on every edge server climbs to 100 percent. Traffic is normal, 502 errors spike worldwide, and engineers cannot reach internal systems that sit behind the same edge.
clues: The deploy was a firewall rule update
CPU is high on every server, in every region
The firewall process is the largest user of CPU in a profile
troubleshoot.question: What is your first action and why?
hints: Think about which change coincides with the start of the problem.
What is the fastest safe way to stop the CPU burn everywhere?
Can you reach the dashboard or API if they also run behind the same edge?
troubleshoot.answer: Disable the firewall rules globally with the kill switch, because the profile and timing both point at it and every minute of delay is a minute of outage. Then check that CPU and 502s fall, investigate the rule offline, and re-enable in stages. Also make sure you have a way into your own tools when the edge is down.

rootcause.q: What is the best one-sentence root cause?
options: A DDoS attack overloaded the network
A new WAF rule with a backtracking regular expression was deployed to all edges without a staged rollout
A routing leak sent traffic to the wrong place
A hardware fault in a data centre
rootcause.why: Cloudflare says a single rule with a poorly written regular expression exhausted CPU, and the procedure allowed it to go global without staging.

remediation.task: Write a CPU-budget test for a new firewall rule.
remediation.answer: Run the rule against a set of long, hostile and typical inputs and fail the build if any input takes longer than a small budget, for example a few milliseconds. Include inputs with no match, because those force the engine to try every path.

remediation.task: Define a staged rollout for rules that still allows an emergency lane.
remediation.answer: Stage 1: a few internal or low-traffic edges. Stage 2: a small percentage. Stage 3: everywhere. Each stage waits a few minutes and checks CPU and errors. An emergency lane skips waiting but not the canary stage, and needs approval from two people.

remediation.task: Decide how customers will learn about the outage when your status page depends on you.
remediation.answer: Publish status from a system outside your own network, update it automatically from health checks, and keep a social account or email list as a second channel.

design.prompt: Design the delivery path for security rules so new rules protect customers quickly but can never take down serving.
constraints: Rules must reach most edges within minutes in an attack
A rule must not be able to use more than a small share of CPU
Operators must be able to disable one rule or all rules fast
design.answer: Use a linear-time matching engine and per-request CPU limits so no single rule can starve serving. Run every rule through a CPU-profile test in the pipeline. Deploy first to a canary group, watch CPU and error rate for a few minutes, then fan out. Keep per-rule and global kill switches with clear ownership, and make the control plane reachable independently of the edge.

checks.q: What made this change reach every server so fast?
options: WAF Managed Rules were deployed globally without the staged rollout used for other software
checks.why: The post says the procedure allowed a non-emergency rule change to go to production worldwide without a staged rollout.

checks.q: Why is a regex that fails to match often more dangerous than one that matches?
options: The engine may try a huge number of paths before giving up
checks.why: With backtracking engines, a failed match can explore many combinations before concluding there is no match.

checks.q: Which fix changes the blast radius?
options: Adding a comment to the rule
checks.why: Staged rollout limits how many servers see a bad rule before CPU alarms stop the rollout.

checks.q: What is a sensible use of a global kill switch during an incident?
options: Use it when diagnosis points at a component and restoring service matters more than temporary loss of that feature
Use it only after a full root-cause report
checks.why: Cloudflare restored traffic within two minutes of disabling the WAF globally. The cost of the delay before the decision was extra minutes of outage.

preventive: Stage every production change, including security rules
Test the performance cost of rules, not only their correctness
Use matching engines with bounded running time
Keep CPU protection that limits any single rule
monitoring: Alert on a fleet-wide CPU jump after a deploy
Correlate alerts with the deploy log automatically
Update the status page automatically from health checks
recovery: Practise using the global kill switch
Keep a path into your own control plane that does not depend on the edge
practices: Fast changes still need guard rails
A tool that must respond to attacks quickly is also a tool that can break everything quickly
Write regular expressions with worst-case inputs in mind
